content.title: About
content.content: Pumpkin pancakes are thin, tender crepes with grated pumpkin, warm spices, and sometimes a splash of cream folded into the batter. The pumpkin gives them a golden‑orange hue, a subtle sweetness, and a cozy autumn aroma. They are commonly served with sour cream, honey, fruit sauce, or a nutty topping.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pumpkin is rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Making pumpkin pancakes is a traditional autumn tradition in Russia and Eastern Europe.
Pumpkin adds few calories, making these pancakes lighter than classic buttery versions.
The pumpkin‑infused batter holds its shape well, resulting in fluffier, softer pancakes.
Whole pumpkins store for 2‑3 months in a cool place; once cut, they should be used within a week.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene from pumpkin supports vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts antioxidant protection and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Pumpkin contributes virtually no saturated fat, making the dish heart‑friendly.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and normal muscle function.

items.title: Pumpkin allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to pumpkin.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Pumpkin is naturally sweet, so those monitoring blood sugar should account for it in their total intake.

items.title: Added ingredients
items.content: When using pre‑made pancake mixes, check for artificial flavors and preservatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pumpkin pancakes hot, rolled or folded. Drizzle with sour cream, honey, maple syrup, or fruit sauce, and sprinkle with nuts or seeds. They pair well with cottage cheese, yogurt, or a mild cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked pancakes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in freezer‑safe bags and reheat in the microwave or on a skillet before serving.

potato-baked-peel-eaten-with-chili.title: Potato, baked, peel eaten, with chili

content.title: About
content.content: Baked potato with the peel left on and a spicy chili sauce is a popular dish that combines a fluffy interior, crisp skin, and a kick of heat. Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is a worldwide staple root vegetable rich in carbohydrates, fiber, and B‑vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The potato skin contains more fiber and antioxidants than the flesh alone.
Baking retains more vitamins, especially vitamin C, compared with boiling.
Chili peppers provide capsaicin, which can boost metabolism and add heat.
Around the world baked potatoes are seasoned with everything from rosemary to paprika.
Potatoes were first domesticated in the Andes over 7,000 years ago.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Potatoes supply slowly digestible starches that help maintain satiety over time.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Fiber in the peel
items.content: The skin adds dietary fiber, beneficial for digestion and blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Capsaicin in chili
items.content: Capsaicin has antioxidant properties and may help increase metabolic rate.

items.title: Minerals: potassium and magnesium
items.content: Potatoes provide potassium for heart and muscle function and magnesium for nerve health.

items.title: Nightshade allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to potatoes or chili.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Baked potatoes can raise blood glucose quickly, so portion control is important for diabetics.

items.title: Spicy chili sauce
items.content: Excessive chili may irritate the stomach in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Too much added salt can increase the risk of hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the baked potato hot, split it open and sprinkle grated chili or drizzle a chili sauce. The skin can be eaten together with the flesh, becoming crisp in the oven. Add a drizzle of olive oil, fresh herbs, or a yogurt dip to balance the heat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw potatoes in a cool, dark place at 7‑10 °C. Cooked baked potatoes are best consumed within 2‑3 days, kept in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Reheat in the oven to restore a crispy skin.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato salad with egg is a classic dish made from boiled potatoes, hard‑boiled eggs, mayonnaise or sour cream, herbs and seasonings. It is commonly served as a snack or side dish in restaurants and homes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The salad is a staple in post‑Soviet cuisine and appears on many café menus.
Traditional recipes often include pickles or mustard for extra flavor.
It can be prepared ahead of time and keeps well in the fridge for 2‑3 days.
Variations may add ham, chicken or seafood.
Garnish with fresh dill, parsley or green onions for color and aroma.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Potatoes provide slowly digestible carbohydrates that supply steady energy and help maintain blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs add complete protein, essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both potatoes and eggs contain B6, B12 and folate, supporting nervous system function.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: When made with vegetable‑oil mayonnaise or sour cream, the salad contains monounsaturated fats.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish provides potassium, phosphorus and iron, which are important for heart and muscle health.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Mayonnaise or sour cream makes the salad calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Adding pickles or store‑bought mayo can increase the salt content.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage can allow bacterial growth, especially because the salad contains eggs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a standalone appetizer or as a side to meat dishes. It can be eaten with a spoon or fork, or used as a filling for sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. Consume within 2‑3 days. Stir before serving to redistribute the dressing.

content.title: About
content.content: Sangria is a traditional Spanish beverage made from red dry wine, fruit, sugar, and sometimes additions such as brandy or sparkling water. It has a bright fruity aroma, moderate sweetness, and a light wine‑derived bitterness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sangria originated in Spain in the 19th century as a way to "dilute" wine and make it more refreshing in hot weather.
Traditional recipes use seasonal fruits: oranges, lemons, apples, peaches, and berries.
Sangria is often served in large pitchers, allowing the fruit to steep in the wine for several hours.
There are many variations: white (based on white wine), rosé, and even non‑alcoholic versions made with fruit juices.
Spanish law limits the alcohol content of commercial sangria to 12 %.

items.title: Antioxidants from wine
items.content: Red wine contains polyphenols such as resveratrol, which may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Vitamins from fruit
items.content: The fruits in sangria provide vitamin C, potassium, and fiber, which aid immunity and digestion.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Adding sparkling water or juice increases the liquid volume, helping maintain hydration.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Sangria contains alcohol, so it should be consumed in moderation, especially by individuals with contraindications.

items.title: Sugar
items.content: Traditional recipes often include added sugar or syrup, raising the drink’s calorie count.

items.title: Fruit allergies
items.content: Some fruits may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve sangria chilled in glasses or tumblers. Let it rest in the refrigerator for 2–4 hours before serving so the fruit flavors fully develop. Add ice and fresh fruit slices for garnish if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared sangria in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. After that, flavor and aroma may deteriorate, and alcohol can evaporate.

content.title: About
content.content: Seven‑layer salad is a multi‑layered lettuce salad that alternates layers of onion, celery, green pepper, peas, mayonnaise, cheese, eggs and/or bacon. The dish is popular in the United States and is often served at holiday gatherings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the distinct visible layers when the salad is sliced.
The classic recipe uses mayonnaise, but modern versions may substitute yogurt or sour cream.
The combination of fresh vegetables and smoky bacon creates a contrast of textures and flavors.
It is frequently garnished with olives, cherry tomatoes, or sliced green onions.
In the U.S. it is a common “potluck” dish at family reunions and picnics.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Onion, celery and green pepper provide vitamin B6 and folate, which support metabolism.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Eggs, cheese and bacon supply complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Lettuce, celery and peas add fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Bacon and mayonnaise (especially when made with olive oil) contribute monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Green pepper and onion contain vitamin C and flavonoids that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Mayonnaise and bacon make the salad calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Bacon and cheese can add significant salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Allergy to eggs or dairy
items.content: Individuals allergic to eggs, cheese or milk should avoid or substitute those ingredients.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: If eggs are not fully cooked, there is a risk of salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the seven‑layer salad chilled, sliced into portions. It can be eaten as a main dish or as a side to meat. Fresh herbs such as parsley or dill may be added for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days maximum. Stir gently before serving to redistribute the mayonnaise.

content.title: About
content.content: Green decaffeinated tea is a leaf tea made from Camellia sinensis whose natural caffeine has been removed. It retains the fresh, slightly grassy flavor of green tea while lacking the stimulating effect of caffeine, making it suitable for evening consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeination is usually performed by steam or CO₂ extraction, preserving most polyphenols.
In Japan, popular varieties such as sencha and matcha are also produced in decaffeinated forms.
The decaffeination process does not change leaf colour – they remain bright green.
Decaffeinated green tea is often used to flavor desserts and beverages.
Unlike black tea, green tea is not fermented, which keeps higher levels of antioxidants.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Leaf green tea contains catechins that help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Regular consumption may help lower LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Metabolism boost
items.content: Some studies suggest catechins can increase metabolic rate and aid weight management.

items.title: Stress reduction
items.content: The amino acid L‑theanine promotes relaxation without causing drowsiness.

items.title: Immune system support
items.content: Polysaccharides and B‑vitamins in tea can strengthen the body’s defenses.

items.title: Tea allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to tea components.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: L‑theanine and polyphenols may affect the action of certain medications, such as anticoagulants.

items.title: Fluoride content
items.content: Excessive consumption can lead to fluoride buildup, which is undesirable for teeth and bones.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place 1‑2 g of leaves in 200‑250 ml of hot (not boiling) water (80‑85 °C) and steep for 2‑3 minutes. Drink plain or add honey, lemon, or milk to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the leaf tea in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Keep it away from moisture and strong odors to preserve aroma and beneficial compounds.
